b: NEW YORK CITY — The inaugural edition of Up/Link: The SpaceTech Business Summit sold out, bringing together the space tech ecosystem at Amazon Web Services in Midtown Manhattan in October 2026.

Designed to be intimate, the first edition was capped at 200 participants including founders, investors and end-users. Up/Link ended its first year in the black and is expected to grow for its second edition in October 2027.
Trade Show Executive (TSE) connected with Up/Link Co-Founder and events entrepreneur Walter Charnizon to find out more about the emerging event.

The driving success behind Up/Link was the ability to convene the companies building real products with potential investors and customers, effectively bringing together professionals across finance, space tech and government.

“I’m used to seeing the same people and companies at every space event. Up/Link was different because it brought investors face to face with smaller companies making real hardware,” stated Gabriel Swiney, Acting Deputy Director of the Office of Space Commerce at the U.S. Department of Commerce. “Building connections between finance and factories is necessary before the space industry can mature, and Up/Link was aimed at that problem more squarely than any other event I’ve attended.”

Due to the quality of the participants, the demand for one-to-one meetings, which were a key feature of the event, outran capacity. The organizing team had to open additional meeting space to accommodate the 1,000-plus meeting requests that came through the platform.
Up/Link was born out of the recognition that a growing amount of venture capital dollars were directed to the space tech industry.

“One of the things I learned doing this early-founder event was that no matter what else founders say, no matter what else start-ups tell you, they’re really only interested in finding capital and customers,” Charnizon said. “So, I decided to launch something here in New York, which is not a space city, but is a capital city. It is a financial and corporate center.”

Knowing what founders were looking for helped Charnizon and his co-founder, Steve Corrick, explore how they were raising large amounts of capital and then design a curated experience to make that connection building easier.

Similar to attendance, in the inaugural year of Up/Link, sponsorships were capped at 12 companies and sold out, signaling the interest the industry has in the event.

“We will have what I think of as controlled growth next year,” Charnizon said. “Attendance will be capped at 250 people, sponsorship at 15 companies, and we expect to prepare for 1,200 meeting requests. We will always protect the intimate, curated nature of Up/Link, and balancing that against the P&L means we have to explore additional market sectors, mechanisms for getting to market and so on. But the scale of Up/Link will be something we manage very closely.”

Future editions of Up/Link will also feature the popular one-to-one meetings program, which were double opt-in, but driven by an algorithm that worked off of individual interests, needs and objectives to ensure the meetings would be time well-spent.
The 2027 edition of the event will also see a continuation of the unstructured networking opportunities the first event facilitated.

“I think direct, one-to-one meetings are increasingly seen as important tools for facilitating meaningful conversations and improving business outcomes for event attendees. But I would be quick to point out that as successful as they can be, setting up meetings like the one-to-one’s we had is just one tool,” Charnizon said. “We also had many windows for social, unstructured networking. I think relying exclusively on one-to-ones is not the right approach.

“It’s sort of like going to the supermarket for a carton of milk. Somehow or other I always get to the checkout line with more in my basket. So, the serendipity of unstructured networking time was also extremely important to the success of the event.”
The Case for Events Industry Entrepreneurship
Up/Link is just one example of the emerging events sprouting up around the country, and the disruption of technology makes the entry of new events into the market all the more likely.

“Up/Link was a cold start. We didn’t have a name in the database or a relationship in the market. I just saw a little piece of blue sky that I thought could be something, and in our first year, we sold out,” Charnizon said. “Because of the way technology works now, because of the way experience can be woven into applications of that technology, it’s a more optimistic time than ever to be in the events business and to start something new.”
